Due to progressive limb bowing with bilateral genu varum, both underwent multiple orthopedic interventions starting at age 7, including femoral and tibial osteotomies with internal fixation, followed by surgical revisions up to age 12.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Intraoral clinical photograph of a buccal fistula adjacent to a primary molar in a pediatric patient with XLH (article title and caption), with intact dentition and no caries or trauma — the classic dental-abscess presentation of XLH. B: Intraoral clinical photograph of a buccal fistula adjacent to a primary molar in the same pediatric XLH patient, with intact dentition — classic XLH dental abscess manifestation. C: Intraoral clinical photograph of a buccal fistula adjacent to a primary molar in the same pediatric XLH patient, with intact dentition — classic XLH dental abscess manifestation. D: Panoramic radiograph of the same pediatric XLH patient showing periapical radiolucency and root resorption in multiple primary molars with intact permanent tooth germs — the radiographic correlate of XLH dental abscesses with apparently intact teeth; red arrows annotate the affected molars.

panels.figure_caption: Intraoral and extraoral photographs and panoramic imaging of the patient showing multiple fistulas and dental pathology: (A) Buccal fistula in the upper right quadrant. (B) Buccal fistula in the lower left quadrant. (C) Buccal fistula in the lower right quadrant. (D) Panoramic radiograph (2024) showing extensive periapical radiolucency and root resorption in multiple primary molars (54, 64, 74, 75, 84, 85).
in_text_mentions: Dental Findings: Clinical and radiographic aspects: Intraoral examination revealed four fistulous openings on the buccal mucosa, located adjacent to the upper left first primary molar (tooth 64), upper right first primary molar (tooth 54), lower left second primary molar (tooth 75), and lower right second primary molar (tooth 85). The gingiva appeared normal, and there were no carious lesions or signs of trauma (Figure 1A–D).

Panoramic radiography (Figure 1D) showed pronounced internal and external root resorption and extensive periapical radiolucency involving several primary molars (54, 64, 74, 75, 84, 85). The lesions measured approximately 2–4 mm, were diffuse, mainly affecting the furcation area and the medial roots, and displayed moderate, irregularly shaped root resorption. B: Bilateral leg radiograph of the same XLH patient showing osteopenic tibia and fibula with an insufficiency fracture at the left tibial diaphysis, per caption and in-text. No vocabulary finding_key matches, so findings are listed as proposed_findings.

in_text_mentions: Preoperative evaluation included Technetium-99 m Sestamibi SPECT imaging as well as a complete thyroid and parathyroid ultrasound. The Sestamibi scan showed focal intense tracer uptake on delayed images in the right tracheoesophageal groove, as well as increased tracer uptake suggestive of an enlarged left sided gland (Figure 2). Ultrasound revealed a normal appearing thyroid gland, with bilateral enlarged superior parathyroid glands in the tracheoesophageal groove. Neither inferior parathyroid gland was visualized (Figure 3).

A: Real human-patient intraoral clinical photograph from the disease-focused article 'A Case of X-Linked Hypophosphatemic Rickets with Dentin Dysplasia in Mandibular Third Molars.' The arrow indicates the right mandibular third molar, which the in-text confirms was impacted at the initial oral examination; these are the teeth harboring the dentin dysplasia that defines this XLH case. Disease attribution rests on the article title together with the specific captioned third-molar manifestation. No vocabulary finding_key applies to this intraoral view (the dental-abscess key is excluded because the caption states no gingival swelling and normal crowns), so the visible impaction is recorded as a proposed finding; because third-molar impaction is nonspecific in itself, confidence is moderated.
